title: Fifth Word Prescribed Prayer And Avoiding Major Sins Opening Comparison

questions.question: What main lesson is this passage trying to teach about prayer and major sins?
questions.answer: It teaches that praying is a true human duty, and staying away from major sins fits the way people were created.

questions.question: In the comparison, what kind of situation were the two soldiers in?
questions.answer: They were in a time when many people were called to military service.

questions.question: How was the first soldier described?
questions.answer: He was trained, careful about his duty, and serious.

questions.question: How was the second soldier described?
questions.answer: He was inexperienced and mostly cared about himself.

questions.question: What did the careful soldier focus on?
questions.answer: He focused on preparing himself and doing his part in the battle.

questions.question: Why did the careful soldier not worry so much about food and supplies?
questions.answer: He knew those things were the responsibility of the state.

questions.question: What kinds of help did he expect from the state if needed?
questions.answer: He expected food, equipment, medical care, and even direct help if he became too weak.

questions.question: What did the careful soldier believe was his own real job?
questions.answer: His real job was training and fighting.

questions.question: Did the careful soldier ever do small jobs with food and equipment? Explain.
questions.answer: Yes. He helped with some of those tasks as part of his service.

questions.question: If someone asked what he was doing during those chores, how did he understand them?
questions.answer: He saw them as duties done for the state.

questions.question: Why did he not think of those chores as working just to feed himself?
questions.answer: Because he believed his living was being provided for him, and those tasks were part of his assigned duty.

questions.question: What can we infer about the attitude of the careful soldier?
questions.answer: He was responsible, trusting, and clear about the difference between his duty and his provision.

questions.question: What does the passage say is suitable for a human being to do?
questions.answer: To perform the prayers and avoid serious sins.

questions.question: What teaching method is used to explain this idea?
questions.answer: A comparison using two soldiers.

questions.question: Where were the two soldiers placed together?
questions.answer: In the same regiment.

questions.question: What is one big difference between the two soldiers?
questions.answer: One was disciplined and duty-minded, while the other was untrained and self-focused.

questions.question: What did the disciplined soldier give his attention to?
questions.answer: He gave his attention to military preparation and the struggle they were in.

questions.question: What did he understand about getting his basic needs?
questions.answer: He understood that the government was supposed to provide them.

questions.question: What shows that the state’s care could go very far?
questions.answer: The passage says the state would even feed him directly if he could not do it himself.

questions.question: Besides training and fighting, what other tasks did the disciplined soldier do?
questions.answer: He helped with practical camp jobs like preparing and cleaning eating things.

questions.question: When he did those camp jobs, how did he describe them?
questions.answer: He described them as service he was doing for the state.

questions.question: What important difference did he make about his work?
questions.answer: He did not see those chores as a way of chasing his own food.

questions.question: What does this tell us about his understanding of duty?
questions.answer: He knew his main mission came first, and other small jobs were only part of serving that mission.

questions.question: According to the passage, what two actions match true human duty?
questions.answer: Doing the prescribed prayers and not falling into major sins.

questions.question: Why does the passage use a soldier example?
questions.answer: It helps readers understand the lesson through a clear everyday picture.

questions.question: What was special about the first soldier’s training?
questions.answer: He had already been prepared well and took his responsibilities seriously.

questions.question: What problem did the second soldier have in his character?
questions.answer: He was centered on himself instead of his duty.

questions.question: What did the first soldier avoid worrying about too much?
questions.answer: He avoided constant worry about food and supplies.

questions.question: What reasons did he have for not worrying?
questions.answer: He believed the state would provide what he needed, care for him when sick, and support him if he became unable.

questions.question: What did the soldier consider his essential responsibility?
questions.answer: Preparing himself and taking part in the fighting.

questions.question: Did he ignore all ordinary tasks related to meals and gear?
questions.answer: No. He still took care of some of them as part of his work.

questions.question: Give two examples of those ordinary tasks.
questions.answer: He prepared cooking items and cleaned eating containers.

questions.question: How did he answer when asked what he was doing?
questions.answer: He said he was carrying out service duties.

questions.question: What answer did he refuse to give about those tasks?
questions.answer: He refused to say he was just working for his own food.

questions.question: What human purpose is being explained in this passage?
questions.answer: The passage explains that worship, especially prayer, is part of why human beings were made.

questions.question: What kind of sins are mentioned as things to avoid?
questions.answer: Serious sins.

questions.question: In the story, what was happening in the country at that time?
questions.answer: There was a broad military call-up.

questions.question: What was the first soldier like in both skill and character?
questions.answer: He was skilled and careful about doing what was right.

questions.question: What was the second soldier like?
questions.answer: He was new, immature, and mainly concerned with himself.

questions.question: What did the first soldier put first in his life as a soldier?
questions.answer: He put training and battle duty first.

questions.question: How did he view food, gear, and medical treatment?
questions.answer: He viewed them as things the state was responsible to provide.

questions.question: What detail shows his trust was very strong?
questions.answer: He believed he would be helped even in a very weak condition.

questions.question: Did his trust make him lazy? Explain.
questions.answer: No. He still did useful service jobs when needed.

questions.question: How did he think about those useful service jobs?
questions.answer: He saw them as assigned duties, not as a personal chase for survival.

questions.question: What false idea did he avoid?
questions.answer: He avoided thinking that his whole purpose was just to earn his food.

questions.question: What does the verse at the beginning say about the people Allah is with?
questions.answer: Allah is with people who are mindful of Him and who do good.

questions.question: What example is used right after the verse?
questions.answer: The example of two soldiers.

questions.question: What was the better soldier busy with?
questions.answer: He was busy with preparation and carrying out his military duty.

questions.question: What was he not deeply anxious about?
questions.answer: He was not deeply anxious about his food and supplies.

questions.question: Why was he calm about those needs?
questions.answer: He trusted that those needs would be taken care of by the state.

questions.question: What kinds of care did he believe were included in that support?
questions.answer: Food, equipment, treatment when sick, and even direct feeding if necessary.

questions.question: What did he say was his main responsibility?
questions.answer: His main responsibility was to train and fight.

questions.question: Did he completely avoid practical chores?
questions.answer: No. He also did some practical camp chores.

questions.question: Name one chore he did.
questions.answer: He cleaned the eating utensils.

questions.question: What did he call those chores when asked about them?
questions.answer: He called them service tasks for the state.

questions.question: What two things does the passage connect together as part of proper human living?
questions.answer: Regular prayer and staying away from major wrongdoing.

questions.question: What kind of story is used to make the lesson easier to understand?
questions.answer: A comparison about two soldiers in the army.

questions.question: What setting brings urgency to the story?
questions.answer: A time of war preparation involving everyone.

questions.question: Which soldier is the good example in the story?
questions.answer: The trained and dutiful soldier.

questions.question: What makes the second soldier a bad example?
questions.answer: He lacks training and thinks mostly about himself.

questions.question: What did the good soldier understand about who provides daily needs?
questions.answer: He understood that the state provides those needs.

questions.question: What was his first priority?
questions.answer: His first priority was to get ready and do his fighting duty.

questions.question: What does this show about the order of responsibilities in his mind?
questions.answer: It shows that mission came first, while food and supplies were secondary.

questions.question: What are some examples of extra tasks he still did?
questions.answer: He helped with cooking-related tools and with cleaning after meals.

questions.question: How did he describe those extra tasks?
questions.answer: He described them as part of his official service.
